commenti.body: I was wondering about the same things. I also noticed that the lawyers seemed free to soliloquize whenever they felt like it. (There was even a joke in the film about this-->!"despite appearances, that was not a closing argument."!<)
Ya that was funny, it seemed the lawyers could monologue whenever they wanted, whether it was their witness or the others

The legal system in France is obviously not like this. It was just a vehicle to let the story develop.

I love the movie but it did go too far on two occasions were it made suspense of disbelief a little hard:

* When the argument is made that she is a murderer because she wrote a book about a murderer.

* When the blood spatter analyst comes in and just says she did it instead of staying on the matter of blood spatter.

Great movie though, because ultimately it's not about the case itself but a study in how a relationship between these people fell apart, and how the father himself fell apart.

I saw this over the weekend. AMAZING film. I'm also American and am also wondering if the depiction of the legal process was relatively accurate, with the assumption that of course it's going to be dramatized to some degree.

**Spoilers ahead**

I felt like some of the courtroom scenes dragged on a bit, to be honest. However, I loved how the film played with the notion of ambiguity. How, if we're given an incomplete data set, sometimes we just need to make a decision to *believe* one way or another, in order to find some semblence of peace. I liked how (apart from the kid and his caretakers) really NONE of the characters were universally "likable." All of them acted selfishly at times, played the victim, took advantage and were generally assholes. So it was very difficult to really root for anyone except the kid. And, even now, I'm unsure whether or not he just made up the entire conversation in the car with his dad in order to find resolution and put the ordeal to rest. I mean, it's plausible and it seems to fit in with the "filling in the blanks" motif of the film. I'd love to hear other theories. I don't think she killed him, but I do think that mayyyyybe the kid made the story up, or at least, the ditector was agile enough to leave that open as a possibility to consider.

Anyway, brilliant film.

Don't know if there are any french lawyers in this sub but criminal procedure can be pretty damn different from country to country. I would say that a lot of those very strict american rules have to do with the significance of the jury. It's a jury trial in the movie too but I assume that in France the judge still has more of a say. Evidence law in the american sense isn't really a concept in continental europe

nah fuck that im tired of great French films with ambiguous endings. I was praying that the ending would be her looking into the camera saying "yeah I killed that bitch" and blasts PIMP.

ok but all jokes aside I fucking knew it was gonna be an ambiguous French ending with a calming activity before the credits roll. great movie nonetheless. 9/10 without ending, 5/10 with ending because I need to know, I just gotta. 10/10 work from the director though because she clearly elicited the intended response from me.

For the ending I also came away wondering if the kid made it up. There was a notable lack of grief or even any detail about the father at all. But given the strange dramatic style over realism for the court scenes, I don't think that the plot goes that deep. I think overall it was a story about how even innocent people can be not good/the hero.

I'm french but not a specialist of the french legal system. The only thing I can say is that:

- Yes, everyone can talk freely (there is no "objection !" in french courts)
- No, a therapist can not break medical confidentiality, even after the death of a patient, and say what this patient told him in session (unless it concerns a murder to come or a risk of child abuse). That's the main weird point in the movie, as everyone knows it, so everyone knows it's false.

In interviews ([like this one](https://www.actu-juridique.fr/professions/anatomie-dune-chute-pose-la-question-aimeriez-vous-etre-juge-comme-ca/)), people from french justice system say that not everything is accurate, but that usually, when it's something which doesn't happen in reality (the fact the attorney general steps down from his perch, the fact to put someone 24h/24h naer the child to protect his testimony...), nothing forbids its in law, and its not contradictory with the spirit of french justice. They basically all agree that the "mood" of a trial, the rythm, the possible chaos and the way people argue with each other, is close to the actual trials.

To see how french trial work, I recommend a very good documentary, "10e chambre instants d'audience" from Depardon (2004), which was one of the first film allowed to film french justice (which is forbidden by law). It's about very little accusations (drunk while driving, etc.), but you see well how it works.

Why was there no discussion of the murder weapon? After the initial reference to a blunt object, there was absolutely no attempt to find the weapon, nor any attempt by the defence to question its absence. This was the most spectacular wtf? for me.

It was very briefly addressed - during the blood spatter expert's testimony I think the defence attorney added a comment to the effect of "you mean the blunt instrument that was never found?" And from memory the prosecutor said something like "we don't often find the weapon".

Ah, thanks! Nonsense, too, as the murder weapon is often found. I suppose that the film signals some movement away from the forensics toward psychology, but this is one of the parts that just felt like too much. Makes it too easy to set up 'when you don't know you have to decide'.
